name: Standing Wave
text: [overview] Next come a thin crack and a bulge (5.9), blockier pitches to a snowpatch of about 35 degrees (rubble late), and blocky 5.6 on an arete to the rim.
[what_to_bring] crampons and ice axe — approach and descent
[approach] The approach is short but steep, and an ice axe, sometimes crampons, are needed on the snow early in the season.
[descent_text] The route finishes on the summit rim after crossing the snowpatch high on the face.
[descent_text] It holds snow early in the season, so carry an ice axe and crampons.
[descent_text] Another option from the rim is the glacier descent, but that slope can shed large blocks in the afternoon.

name: The Tuning Fork
text: [overview] A long alpine line approached from the slab bivy: cross a snow patch to a corner system right of the base.
[approach] Climb the slash at the toe of the feature, bypass a slot canyon with snow, and climb a short pitch up a face to a bushy ledge.
[approach] Cross snow and wet slabs to the bivy basin below the wall.
[descent_text] From the top, walk the ridgeline toward Ratney and descend into the col, then scramble through blocks just left of the first big snow patch to the summit of Ratney.
[descent_text] From there skirt the snow heading northeast toward the rib on the north end of the basin that holds lower Statlu Lake.

[descent_text] Several rappels reach the flatter, snowy part of the ridge, then more lead to a ledge with two snow patches on the second southern-facing offshoot, and a last rappel from a tree puts you on the slabs.
[descent_text] Snow and wet slabs lead back to camp.

name: North Ridge via North Glacier
text: [overview] A steep forest trail leads to a campsite at tree line, then the route crosses a small crevassed glacier to an exposed ledge that gives onto the easy north ridge.
[overview] The ridge ends at a snow wall with a cornice near the top.
[beta] From the campsite, go up alpine slabs to the glacier and cross it, watching for crevasses.
[beta] Reach the ledge on the east side of the glacier;
[beta] Beyond the ledge the north ridge is easy scrambling on solid quartzite to a final snow wall and cornice below the summit.
[hazards] Crevasses on a heavily crevassed small glacier.
[hazards] Moat or bergschrund at the glacier edge.
[hazards] Cornice near the summit
[watch_out] The glacier has shrunk, making the ledge access harder than older descriptions
[gear] Crampons.
[gear] Ice axe.
[gear] Glacier rescue gear
[approach] the glacier starts about a kilometre beyond it.
[descent_text] The usual descent goes down the east ridge on rock and steep snow to the col, then a steep north couloir to the glacier.

name: Stanford Route
text: [approach] Climbers start from a high camp at the saddle northeast of the peak, from which a snow ridge rises to a subsummit.

name: Athabasca Glacier to East Face
text: [overview] Head up the Athabasca Glacier from the tour parking area to the Columbia Icefield, threading between large crevasses in the middle of the glacier while avoiding the serac fall that often comes from Snowdome toward the climber's-right side.
[detailed_rack] Usual crevasse-rescue and glacier-travel equipment.

name: Brohm Ridge/NE Face
text: [overview] Follows Brohm Ridge to the Garibaldi Neve and the North Pitt Glacier, then climbs the NE face to Garibaldi's 8776 ft summit.
[what_to_bring] ice axe.
[what_to_bring] crampons.
[what_to_bring] glacier kit — crevasse rescue
[approach] Take Highway 99 from Squamish to the Cheekye forest road and follow it and its Brohm Ridge branch as far as snow or the road end allows;
[approach] Drop onto the Warren Glacier and cross it, roped, then continue over the North Pitt Glacier to the flat bench at the foot of the northeast face.
[approach] Crevasses and seracs are present and snowmobile traffic is common on the lower road.
[descent_text] Go back down the northeast face by the way you came up, watching for the bergschrund and for cornices along the upper edges.
[descent_text] Rope up again where the glaciers are crevassed, then retrace the route across the glaciers and west along Brohm Ridge.
[descent_text] Late in the day the snow on the ridge can be sticky and the many small ups and downs slow progress.

name: North Face Ramp, Winter
text: [overview] This North Shore winter line climbs sustained 45-55 degree snow slopes on the ramp.
[detailed_rack] Pickets for crossing the traverse;
[approach] The ramp is steep and funnels snow, so check the avalanche forecast.
[descent_text] large cornices can sit along the upper part in winter.

name: Herdman Couloir
text: [overview] The easiest way up Macdonald, a snow couloir.
[overview] Spring, while the gully is full of snow, is the preferred time, since otherwise the alders are a slog.
[overview] Glissade the way down while trying to avoid rocks.

name: Northwest Ridge Integral
text: [approach] Leave the car on the highway's south shoulder, east of the Hermit lot and short of the avalanche snowshed.
[approach] Climb the couloir, which is moderate with an axe and crampons when snow-filled and an unpleasant scramble when dry;
[approach] it holds snow into early summer.

name: South Face Rib
text: [approach] Camp above the Houston Glacier, or near Houston Lake if the Melville Glacier is not dropping ice into it.
[approach] The first technical ground is a northeast-trending crossing of the Melville Glacier to the foot of the rib.

name: North Face Couloir
text: [overview] Cross the creek from the logging road at Centre Creek and ascend the gully (ideally snow-filled) to the basin with a pocket glacier beneath the Spires.
[overview] Get over a bergschrund that is tricky, then go up Priest-Coupe, the couloir lying between Rexford and the South Nesakwatch Spire.

[overview] Roughly 80 m short of its top, break left up a narrow slot or chimney for one pitch, then go left across ice bulges, following a snow runnel that opens out, to join the NE ridge high up, with 70 m left to the summit.
[detailed_rack] a picket or two;
[approach] Reach the Centre Creek logging road and cross the creek, then follow the gully, which may be snow-filled, into the basin above the pocket glacier below the Nesakwatch Spires.
[approach] Cross the bergschrund and climb the couloir between Rexford and South Nesakwatch Spire.

name: Priest-Coupe (NE Couloir)
text: [overview] Bergschrunds pose the main technical problem, calling for brief mixed or vertical-snow moves to get over them.
[overview] Gear may be placeable in the couloir walls, though big moats can develop later in the season.
[overview] Snow and ice can fall from the walls overhead.

name: West Ridge
text: [approach] The ridge is mainly scrambling with a few fifth-class sections, and no glacier travel is needed.
[descent_text] It alternates between snow and rock, with krummholz to push through and a few short rappels, and it ends in a basin on the Centre Creek side, well away from the Nesakwatch approach.

name: Emperor Ridge
text: [overview] A serious, committing ridge whose difficulty depends heavily on the state of the snow gargoyles;
[overview] if the snow is bad, retreat is the only option.
[detailed_rack] Some ice and snow gear plus a modest rock rack.

name: Kain Face
text: [overview] The first route up Mount Robson, and now probably its safest, since the serac that once threatened the face has wasted away.
[overview] Snow and ice of moderate to steep angle on the Kain Face lead to easier faces and ice gargoyles below a large summit.
[detailed_rack] Ice screws, pickets and a V-thread kit.
[approach] Parties also fly to the Extinguisher and cross the glacier to the same camp at the Dome.

name: Patterson Couloir
text: [overview] It could give a fast way toward the foot of the Kain Face in spring, once deep snow covers the brush, the Dome's rocks are plastered in place and avalanches have scoured the couloir.

name: Roof Glacier Hourglass By-Pass Couloir
text: [overview] Ascends immediately to the right of the Hourglass Couloir on the Roof Glacier's right side, eventually arriving atop the Kain Face.
[approach] From the Forster Hut, go past the first icefall above, then turn uphill onto the neve of the Roof Glacier.
[approach] Continue to the rock band and look for the hidden gully that cuts through it, leading to the steep snow slope to the top of the Kain Face.

name: South Face/Schwartz Ledges
text: [descent_text] With enough snow, the steep upper slopes can be downclimbed to the Schwartz Ledges.
[descent_text] Some parties stay above the ice cliff, descend the glacier and make one or two long rappels to reach the ridge above Little Robson.
[descent_text] Otherwise reverse the ledge traverse beneath the calving serac, then reverse the ascent route.

name: The North Face
text: [overview] the crossing depends strongly on conditions and may be dangerous, and an alternative is walking up and crossing where the Robson Glacier ends.
[overview] Step onto Berg Glacier close to its toe and ascend the small icefall into the bowl beneath the face.

[overview] About 14 to 18 pitches of 50 degree ice and snow lead to the Emperor Ridge and summit.

[approach] Cross the Robson River upstream of the lake, or go farther up and cross over the Robson Glacier's snout.
[approach] Step onto the Berg Glacier close to its end and climb a minor icefall to the bowl at the base of the face.

name: Coldwell Creek Couloir
text: [overview] Cross to the foot of the narrow couloir and climb it, up to about 45 degrees at its steepest, until it opens into a wider snow slope at the saddle by Pump Peak.
[detailed_rack] Pickets or screws only for roping up.

name: Not-so-grand Sorta-central (NS) Couloir
text: [overview] A steep snow gully with several mixed steps, a fun outing when snow is thin;
[overview] it was climbed in about 40 cm of snow.
[overview] P1 (M4-) opens with an M3 bouldery step, then steep snow and then a second, longer bouldery step at M4-, and belays at a tree on the right.
[overview] P2 (M2) climbs a steep snow ramp, ending at a belay from pitons on the left side.
[approach] The hut itself is a couple of hours from the summer parking, longer in deep snow.

text: [overview] snow pockets can raise the grade.

[approach] A wilderness pass is needed for backcountry camping, and snow on the slopes below the col may call for an ice axe and crampons early in the season.

[descent_text] Below the last of the face stations, scree and ledges lead to slab or snow at the base of a dihedral, then two more rappels or 4th-class downclimbing reach the scree trail back to the Uto-Sir Donald col.

text: [what_to_bring] ice axe — early season, for snow on the way in and out

name: North face
text: [overview] The bergschrund is crossed near the center, followed by snow gullies steeper than 60 degrees, snice on sloping granite and rock bands of fourth class, straight up to the crest, which is reached slightly east of the summit.

name: Northwest ridge
text: [overview] Approach as for the north face, then cross the glacier to the northwest ridge on the right.
[overview] Reach the top via third-class rock, plus snow of moderate steepness just left of the crest.
[what_to_bring] ice tools — two help on the snow bulges;
[what_to_bring] one ice axe works but is less secure

name: West Ridge
text: [approach] Walk up from the Hermit parking area to Hermit Meadows, then follow cairns and a faint beaten path through meadows and past waterfalls to a low point on the west ridge above the Tupper glacier, the Tupper shoulder.

name: Southwest Face
text: [beta] Reach a snow ridge and then the crux wall of small ledges below the summit block;
[hazards] Hard snow ridge.

[gear] Crampons for the snow ridge.
[descent_text] Descend the same route, downclimbing the crux wall carefully, then glissade or plunge-step snow patches and descend the long loose rubble of the lower gully.
[turnaround] Turn back if snow on the ridge is too hard to cross safely or if water and daylight are running low in the heat.
[pitch_detail] Steep, very loose rubble slopes to a snow ridge..

name: Bravo Glacier to Southeast Chimney
text: [overview] Early summer is safer on the Bravo Glacier, yet chunks of ice may still fall from the summit tower;
[overview] later the tower is clear but crevasses open, pushing parties toward the flanks and into avalanche exposure.

[overview] Aim to cross the southeast rib on the side nearest Bravo Peak, as far toward it as is safe, reach the col between Bravo and Spearman, then cover two kilometers of glacier and 1,700 feet of steeper snow to the Tooth.

[overview] Cross the bergschrund, take a fourth class ramp right to the notch, and follow a narrow ridge to the chimney: about 250 feet of fifth class past three chockstones, the third being the crux.
[approach] Most parties are flown in and land on Rainy Knob beside the Tiedemann Glacier, because large crevasses make a landing on the glacier itself impractical.
[approach] The route then follows the Bravo Glacier, passing about midway between the east ridge of Bravo Peak and the smaller southeast rib.
[approach] Crossing the rib, which closes the glacier into a cul-de-sac, is the main glacier problem;
[descent_text] A final rappel gets you past the bergschrund at its foot.

name: Kiwi Route
text: [overview] Rib of snow and ice up the North Face, which is otherwise threatened;
[overview] it ends at a snow ramp beneath the summit tower, and the usual finish is the notch chimney.
[overview] Cross a debris field briefly, then the bergschrund near 9900', beyond which the overhead hazard ends.
[overview] Ice at 45 to 60 degrees for 800 feet gives way to an arete of 50 degree snow, a short icefall and gentler snow.
[approach] From a camp on the col, walk a few minutes through a debris field to the bergschrund, near 9,900 ft, and cross it as far left as you can to stay clear of the seracs.
[approach] Steep ice leads from there to a snow arete.

[descent_text] Reversing the route with extensive downclimbing is possible, but the usual way down is to rappel the summit tower, go up a brief couloir onto the northwest summit shoulder, then descend the Angel Glacier.
[descent_text] Most of this is walking, though finding the easy line through the icefall takes some searching, and several sections lie under active seracs.

name: McNerthney Pillar
text: [overview] Above the third pillar, snow and ice lead up through the big overhanging serac bands guarding the Angel Glacier.
[approach] It crosses the bergschrund to reach the first of three pillars on the north face of Waddington.

name: Northeast Spur (PD+)
text: [overview] Difficulties are mainly on the snow apron at 45 degrees below the rock, where many lines are possible;

[detailed_rack] Axe and crampons;

name: Massey's
text: [overview] Once the first ice section ends the angle relents: either belay and bring up the second, or continue through more ice to a snowfield, then go left around it and anchor on good ice (one 70 m rope covers all this in a single pitch).

name: Ice caves at the Skillet Glacier
grade: 5.0 V16 WI1 M1 C0 Easy Snow

name: North Face
text: [overview] A steep band at the base leads to a large low-angle shield of heather or snow, with another steep band near the top.
[overview] Climbed in summer (solo), when it is heathery with poor climbing, and in winter, when it has two distinct cruxes around M4 separated by frozen heather and steep snow that is not hard.
[detailed_rack] Some gear helps in winter: pieces that can be driven into frozen heather or a crack filled with snow and ice without pulling out, such as hexes, tri-cams and spectres.

name: North Nesakwatch Spire - Nesakwatch Notch (NE Buttress)
text: [overview] Conditions are tricky: snow must fill the notch, after which the climbing is rock.
[overview] Reach it from Centre Creek by crossing the stream and ascending a snow gully to the basin, as on Rexford's north face.
[overview] go up snow beneath the chockstone that stands alone, then downclimb one pitch beyond, under the N face.
[detailed_rack] also ice tools, crampons and snow/ice protection.
[approach] Ford the creek, then go up a snow gully into the basin, the same way as the Rexford north face.
[approach] The route depends on snow through the notch, so conditions matter.
[descent_text] Early in the season snow on this ridge can make it hazardous.

name: North Nesakwatch Spire - NW Face to W Ridge
text: [overview] From the bottom of the NW face, a ramp slanting across (snow and rock, 4th class) leads up to the west ridge beneath its 5.7 crack pitch, then stay on the ridge to the summit.
[detailed_rack] in early season bring an ice axe and crampons.
[approach] from its base a diagonal ramp of fourth-class rock and snow leads to the upper west ridge.
[approach] In early season bring crampons and an ice axe.
[descent_text] Early in the season snow on this ridge can make it hazardous.

name: South Spire - East Buttress
text: [overview] Getting there means plodding far over snow, so it is best early in the season;
[overview] the approach requires an ice axe and crampons for each climber.
[approach] Ford it and go up the snow gully, toward the Priest-Coupe couloir that separates Rexford from the South Spire.
[approach] Where the couloir meets its bergschrund, step right onto the rock.
[approach] Crampons and ice axes are required, and the route is best early in the season.
[descent_text] Descend the steep sandy gully from the notch, class 2 to 3 or snow-filled early in the season, back to the basin.

name: East Ridge
text: [hazards] Snow or glacier cover early in the season
[gear] Ice axe and crampons if snow or ice remains

name: Arete Du Phalanx (Phalanx South Arete)
text: [overview] The initial half is mostly 3rd/4th class, snow or rock, ending at a prominent spire: sling it, then either rappel or downclimb, and cross steep snow rightward.
[overview] Beyond, the narrow aesthetic arete (low 5th) can be bypassed by an easier traverse, up and to the right across steep snow.
[overview] The final ridge brings further steep snow plus easy mixed ground.

name: South Face Variation
text: [overview] Spring ascents will find the cracks iced and snowy, so consider an ice axe;
[approach] From the Sphinx (Burton) Hut on the southeast side of Garibaldi Lake, climb glaciated terrain to the ridge.

name: Fingerberry Jam
text: [overview] Begin on a snow slope below a left-arching fingercrack.
[approach] Start on a snow slope at a short dyke that leads to the left-arching finger crack.

name: Lentils or TVP, eh?
text: [descent_text] From the summit, downclimb east along the ridge to slings for a short rappel onto broken ground, from which the Crack of Noon route or a snow descent can be reached.

name: Cooper-Kor
text: [approach] The east face is plainly visible from the Bugaboo Glacier.
[approach] Follow the climbers' trail west over loose rock to the Bugaboo Glacier, passing below the south side of Snowpatch Spire.
[approach] Continue up the glacier, staying a little south of Pigeon Spire to avoid large crevasses, then traverse north above them and drop into a small bergschrund to reach the start of the route.
[descent_text] Reverse that ridge, with short rappels as needed, to the low point, then descend the Upper Vowell Glacier side and return over the Bugaboo-Snowpatch col to the hut.
